briefs.problem: Leave requests can stall indefinitely when the assigned manager is unavailable to approve them, with no defined fallback.
briefs.solution: An escalation path added to the leave-approval workflow that reassigns a stuck request when the manager can't act.

challenges.headline: "Manager is away" left undefined
challenges.premise: The request treats 'escalate if the manager is away' as a self-evident trigger.
challenges.alternative: Tying the trigger to the manager's own recorded absence status (already tracked in the absence module) is a synchronous, verifiable condition; a response-timeout after N days is a different, asynchronous mechanism with retries and a visible pending state. These are not interchangeable and the request doesn't say which.
challenges.consequence: Building the wrong trigger means either escalating during a normal offline moment (false positives) or leaving requests stuck for days waiting on a timeout when the manager's absence was already known in the system.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client whether escalation should key off recorded manager absence, a fixed timeout, or both, before designing the workflow.

challenges.headline: Escalation target unspecified
challenges.premise: The request assumes there is an obvious person to escalate to.
challenges.alternative: A named per-manager delegate, a skip-level manager, or HR are three structurally different targets, each with different permission and notification implications, and the platform's client-specific approval circuits suggest this may need to vary by team or country rather than being a single fixed rule.
challenges.consequence: Without this decision, permissions and notification routing can't be built at all, and a hardcoded single target will likely need rework once client-specific circuits are requested.
challenges.recommendation: Settle the escalation-target model (delegate vs. skip-level vs. HR, fixed vs. configurable) with the client before touching permissions or notifications.

challenges.headline: Race between late approval and escalation
challenges.premise: The request implicitly treats escalation as a clean, one-way handoff.
challenges.alternative: Defining explicitly which decision wins when the original manager acts just after escalation fires — and notifying both parties regardless — turns an undefined race condition into a specified, testable rule.
challenges.consequence: Left unaddressed, this is the first thing that breaks in production: two approvers can act on the same request, producing conflicting or duplicate outcomes on a compliance-sensitive record.
challenges.recommendation: Specify the tie-break rule and notification behavior for this race condition as part of the workflow design, not after testing surfaces it.

configurable escalation rules per team/country on a multi-client platform

Route escalation notifications through the existing Contact-role model rather than a bespoke mechanism, for consistency with how the platform already targets billing/HR/operational contacts.

challenges.headline: 'Manager away' detection unspecified
challenges.premise: The request assumes the system can simply tell when a manager is 'away' and escalate.
challenges.alternative: Detecting unavailability automatically from the manager's own approved Absence record reuses existing data and needs no new UI, but couples the escalation logic to the same module it's meant to fix — a manager on unrecorded leave, or with a pending (not yet approved) absence, breaks the trigger. A manual 'delegate my approvals' flag is more reliable but adds a step no one has asked the manager to do.
challenges.consequence: Building either mechanism on the wrong assumption means redoing the trigger logic and the escalation UI once the real expectation surfaces in testing.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client whether detection should be automatic (from Absence data) or manually flagged before touching the workflow.

challenges.headline: Single fallback approver assumed
challenges.premise: The request implies one escalation path, but says nothing about who the fallback approver is or whether that differs by team/country.
challenges.alternative: Given that approval circuits are already explicitly client-specific configuration on this platform, treating the escalation target as configurable (delegate, manager's manager, or HR, settable per team/country) avoids a second wave of work when the first non-standard team appears.
challenges.consequence: Hardcoding a single global escalation target contradicts the platform's own configurability model and forces a rebuild the moment a client needs a different rule per department or country.
challenges.recommendation: Decide now whether escalation target is global or configurable, and model it the same way as existing approval-circuit configuration.

challenges.headline: Escalation timing mechanic undefined
challenges.premise: The request reads as if escalation just 'happens' when the manager is away, without saying whether it fires immediately or after a wait.
challenges.alternative: A timeout-based escalation (fire after N hours/days of no response) is a different, asynchronous build — with a pending state, a scheduled job, and a rule for what happens if the manager returns mid-window — than an immediate, synchronous reroute the moment unavailability is detected.
challenges.consequence: Picking the wrong mechanic late means retrofitting a scheduler and a pending state, or conversely stripping out unneeded async machinery.
challenges.recommendation: Settle immediate-vs-timeout escalation with the client, and check it against any statutory response-time constraint on leave approval.

permissions and notification routing for a new approver role are currently undefined

risks: Approval-circuit and permission code is shared across modules; a change here can ripple into contract or mission approval screens.
Using the manager's own Absence record to trigger escalation creates a circular dependency between the feature and the data it reads.
Undefined escalation-approver permissions risk over-exposing HR-sensitive leave details to a fallback approver who shouldn't see them.
No stated audit trail for escalated approvals, despite labor-law sensitivity on leave — retrofitting it later is expensive.

challenges.headline: Manager-away detection undefined
challenges.premise: The request assumes escalation can reliably detect that 'the manager is away' without specifying what signal drives it.
challenges.alternative: Since the platform already tracks Absence records, keying the trigger off the manager's own approved leave avoids building a separate out-of-office or presence flag from scratch.
challenges.consequence: Without a defined source, the team either builds a parallel, manually-maintained availability flag (fragile, easily stale) or ships escalation that never reliably fires.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client whether the manager's own logged Absence record is an acceptable trigger before designing the detection logic.

challenges.headline: Dual-approver race condition
challenges.premise: The request implies escalation adds a second approver without saying whether the original manager can still act once escalation has fired.
challenges.alternative: Treating escalation as a state transition that revokes the original manager's approve/reject rights — rather than simply adding a parallel approver — keeps ownership of the pending decision unambiguous at any moment.
challenges.consequence: Leaving both approvers active risks conflicting decisions (approve and reject within seconds of each other) with no clear rule for which one wins, and no clean audit story for HR.
challenges.recommendation: Define escalation explicitly as a lock-and-handoff, not an additive second approver, before building the workflow states.

challenges.headline: Escalation policy assumed global
challenges.premise: The request reads as one universal escalation rule, but this platform's approval circuits are normally client- or team-specific.
challenges.alternative: Modeling the escalation delay and target as configurable per team/department from the start costs little extra now and matches how every other approval circuit on this platform already behaves.
challenges.consequence: Hardcoding a single global rule risks a costly retrofit the moment one department wants a different delay or a different backup than another — and approval-circuit changes are known to ripple across shared screens.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm configurability scope with the client even if the first release ships a single default policy.

decisions.decision: Escalation extends the existing leave approval circuit rather than introducing a separate approval system.
decisions.why: Reusing the current workflow avoids duplicating balance checks and notification logic already built for standard approval.
decisions.alternative: Building a standalone escalation mechanism outside the approval circuit.
decisions.tradeoff: Tighter coupling to the existing circuit's states, in exchange for avoiding a parallel, harder-to-maintain approval path.

decisions.decision: Escalation applies only to the manager-approval step of a leave request, not to other approval types on the platform.
